diagnostic_tests.name: A1C
diagnostic_tests.source_text: Diabetes can be diagnosed by demonstrating increased concentrations of glucose in venous plasma or increased A1C in the blood.

diagnostic_tests.name: Fasting Plasma Glucose
diagnostic_tests.source_text: Plasma glucose criteria include either the fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-h plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS]) (Table 2.1).

diagnostic_tests.name: 2-h Plasma Glucose
diagnostic_tests.source_text: Plasma glucose criteria include either the fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-h plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS]) (Table 2.1).

diagnostic_tests.name: Oral Glucose Tolerance Test
diagnostic_tests.source_text: Plasma glucose criteria include either the fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-h plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS]) (Table 2.1).

diagnostic_tests.name: Random Plasma Glucose
diagnostic_tests.source_text: In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L).

diagnostic_tests.name: Islet autoantibodies
diagnostic_tests.source_text: Screen for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes by testing autoantibodies against insulin (IA), glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), islet antigen 2 (IA-2), or zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8). B

diagnostic_tests.name: C-peptide test
diagnostic_tests.source_text: A C-peptide test is only indicated in people receiving insulin treatment.

conditions.name: Diabetes
conditions.source_text: Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders of carbohydrate metabolism in which glucose is both underutilized as an energy source and overproduced due to inappropriate gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, resulting in hyperglycemia (1).

conditions.name: Type 1 diabetes
conditions.source_text: Diabetes is classified conventionally into several clinical categories (e.g., type 1 or type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes mellitus, and other specific types derived from other causes, such as monogenic diabetes, exocrine pancreatic disorders, and high-risk medications) (2).

conditions.name: Type 2 diabetes
conditions.source_text: Type 2 diabetes accounts for 90–95% of all diabetes cases and encompasses individuals who generally have relative (rather than absolute) insulin deficiency in association with insulin resistance (i.e., decreased biological responses to insulin).
conditions.classification: Insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency

conditions.name: Gestational diabetes mellitus
conditions.source_text: Gestational diabetes mellitus (diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes prior to gestation or other types of diabetes occurring throughout pregnancy, such as type 1 diabetes)

conditions.name: Prediabetes
conditions.source_text: Prediabetes is the term used to identify glucose or A1C levels that do not meet the criteria for diabetes yet fall in an intermediate range between normoglycemia and diabetes (25,83).

conditions.name: Impaired Fasting Glucose
conditions.source_text: IFG is defined as FPG levels from 100 to 125 mg/dL (from 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L) (76,82)

conditions.name: Impaired Glucose Tolerance
conditions.source_text: and IGT as 2-h PG levels during 75-g OGTT from 140 to 199 mg/dL (from 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L) (10).

conditions.name: Hyperglycemia
conditions.source_text: Diabetes mellitus is a group of metabolic disorders of carbohydrate metabolism in which glucose is both underutilized as an energy source and overproduced due to inappropriate gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, resulting in hyperglycemia (1).

conditions.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
conditions.source_text: Plasma glucose criteria include either the fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-h plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS]) (Table 2.1).

conditions.name: Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state
conditions.source_text: Plasma glucose criteria include either the fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-h plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss) or hyperglycemic crises (i.e., diabetic ketoacidosis [DKA] and/or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state [HHS]) (Table 2.1).

conditions.name: Monogenic diabetes
conditions.source_text: Diabetes is classified conventionally into several clinical categories (e.g., type 1 or type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes mellitus, and other specific types derived from other causes, such as monogenic diabetes, exocrine pancreatic disorders, and high-risk medications) (2).

conditions.name: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes
conditions.source_text: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) is a common comorbidity in people living with cystic fibrosis that is distinct from type 1 or type 2 diabetes and is often accompanied by pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (144).

conditions.name: Post-transplantation diabetes mellitus
conditions.source_text: Several terms are used in the literature to describe the presence of diabetes following organ transplantation (157). New-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT) is one such designation that describes individuals who develop new-onset diabetes following transplant.

conditions.name: Neonatal diabetes
conditions.source_text: Diabetes occurring under 6 months of age is termed neonatal diabetes, and about 80–85% of cases can be found to have an underlying monogenic cause (32,172–175).

conditions.name: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young
conditions.source_text: MODY is frequently characterized by onset of hyperglycemia at an early age (classically before age 25 years, although diagnosis may occur at older ages).

conditions.name: Immune checkpoint inhibitor–induced autoimmune diabetes
conditions.source_text: The introduction of immunotherapy, specifically immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), for cancer treatment has led to unexpected adverse events, including immune system activation precipitating autoimmune disease.

screening_frequencies.name: Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes screening in asymptomatic adults
screening_frequencies.source_text: In people without prediabetes or diabetes after screening, repeat screening recommended at a minimum of 3-year intervals is reasonable, sooner with symptoms or change in risk (e.g., weight gain). C
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Asymptomatic adults without prediabetes or diabetes

screening_frequencies.name: Prediabetes or Type 2 Diabetes screening in asymptomatic children and adolescents
screening_frequencies.source_text: If tests are normal, repeat testing at a minimum of 3-year intervals (or more frequently if BMI is increasing or risk factor profile is deteriorating) is recommended.
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Asymptomatic children and adolescents with overweight or obesity and risk factors

screening_frequencies.name: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes screening
screening_frequencies.source_text: Current guidelines recommend screening for CFRD in people living with cystic fibrosis starting at age 10 years.
screening_frequencies.applies_to: People with cystic fibrosis starting at age 10 years

screening_frequencies.name: Gestational diabetes mellitus screening
screening_frequencies.source_text: Screen for GDM at 24–28 weeks of gestation in pregnant individuals not previously found to have diabetes or high-risk abnormal glucose metabolism detected earlier in the current pregnancy.
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Pregnant individuals not previously found to have diabetes or high-risk abnormal glucose metabolism

screening_frequencies.name: Postpartum screening for prediabetes or diabetes after GDM
screening_frequencies.source_text: Screen individuals with GDM for prediabetes or diabetes at 4–12 weeks postpartum, using the 75-g OGTT and clinically appropriate non-pregnancy diagnostic criteria.

screening_frequencies.name: Lifelong screening for prediabetes or diabetes after GDM
screening_frequencies.source_text: Individuals with a history of GDM should have lifelong screening for the development of prediabetes or diabetes every 1–3 years.
screening_frequencies.applies_to: Individuals with a history of GDM

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for hyperglycemia in people treated with second-generation antipsychotic medications
screening_frequencies.source_text: People treated with these agents should be screened for prediabetes or diabetes at baseline, re-screened 12–16 weeks after medication initiation, and annually thereafter (112).
screening_frequencies.applies_to: People treated with second-generation antipsychotic medications (after baseline and 12-16 week screening)

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for diabetes and prediabetes in people with HIV
screening_frequencies.source_text: If initial screening results are normal, FPG should be checked annually.
screening_frequencies.applies_to: People with HIV with normal initial screening results

screening_frequencies.name: Screening for diabetes after acute pancreatitis
screening_frequencies.source_text: Screen people for diabetes within 3–6 months following an episode of acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter.

target_goals.name: A1C target for nonpregnant adults
target_goals.source_text: The ADA “Standards of Care in Diabetes” includes the ADA’s current clinical practice recommendations and is intended to provide the components of diabetes care, general treatment goals and guidelines, and tools to evaluate quality of care.

patient_profiles.name: Adults with overweight or obesity and risk factors
patient_profiles.source_text: Testing for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic people should be considered in adults of any age with overweight or obesity who have one or more risk factors for diabetes. B

patient_profiles.name: Asymptomatic adults without prediabetes or diabetes
patient_profiles.source_text: In people without prediabetes or diabetes after screening, repeat screening recommended at a minimum of 3-year intervals is reasonable, sooner with symptoms or change in risk (e.g., weight gain). C

patient_profiles.name: Children and adolescents with overweight or obesity and risk factors
patient_profiles.source_text: Risk-based screening for prediabetes or type 2 diabetes should be considered after the onset of puberty or after 10 years of age, whichever occurs earlier, in children and adolescents with overweight (BMI ≥85th percentile) or obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile) and who have one or more risk factors for diabetes. B
patient_profiles.bmi_range: ≥85th percentile for overweight, ≥95th percentile for obesity

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with a history of GDM
patient_profiles.source_text: Individuals with a history of GDM should have lifelong screening for the development of prediabetes or diabetes every 1–3 years.

patient_profiles.name: People with HIV
patient_profiles.source_text: People living with HIV are at higher risk for developing prediabetes and diabetes. In addition, some antiretroviral (ARV) therapies may further increase the risk.

patient_profiles.name: People treated with second-generation antipsychotic medications
patient_profiles.source_text: In people with HIV, plasma glucose criteria are preferred to diagnose prediabetes and diabetes (17).

patient_profiles.name: People treated with certain medications
patient_profiles.source_text: Screening for prediabetes or diabetes should be performed in people treated with certain medications, such as glucocorticoids, statins (102), thiazide diuretics, some HIV medications (103), and second-generation antipsychotic medications (104), as these drug classes increase the risk of glucose abnormalities, often by promoting insulin resistance.

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with cystic fibrosis
patient_profiles.source_text: Cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) is a common comorbidity in people living with cystic fibrosis that is distinct from type 1 or type 2 diabetes and is often accompanied by pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (144).

patient_profiles.name: Pregnant individuals
patient_profiles.source_text: In individuals who are planning pregnancy, screen those with risk factors (Table 2.5) B and consider testing all individuals of childbearing potential for undiagnosed prediabetes or diabetes. E

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with a family history of type 1 diabetes
patient_profiles.source_text: Autoantibody-based screening for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes should be offered to those with a family history of type 1 diabetes or otherwise known elevated genetic risk. B

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with elevated genetic risk for type 1 diabetes
patient_profiles.source_text: Autoantibody-based screening for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes should be offered to those with a family history of type 1 diabetes or otherwise known elevated genetic risk. B
comorbidities: elevated genetic risk for type 1 diabetes

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with one or more islet autoantibodies
patient_profiles.source_text: Individuals with screening results positive for one or more islet autoantibodies should be evaluated for stage 3 (overt) type 1 diabetes (using A1C, urinalysis, and/or plasma glucose), which would require prompt clinical management and education. B

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with multiple confirmed islet autoantibodies
patient_profiles.source_text: Individuals with multiple confirmed islet autoantibodies and without overt type 1 diabetes have a high risk for progression to stage 3 type 1 diabetes and should be referred to a specialized center for metabolic staging (Table 2.4), education, and consideration of prevention trials or approved treatments (e.g., teplizumab). B

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with a single confirmed IA-2 autoantibody
patient_profiles.source_text: Individuals with a single confirmed IA-2 autoantibody should be monitored similarly to individuals with multiple islet autoantibodies, as IA-2 autoantibody positivity is an independent risk factor for progression. B

patient_profiles.name: Individuals with a single confirmed islet autoantibody
patient_profiles.source_text: Individuals with a single confirmed islet autoantibody should undergo repeat antibody testing every 6 months to 3 years (depending on age) to assess for persistence or seroconversion. E

patient_profiles.name: Adults with phenotypic risk factors that overlap with type 1 diabetes
patient_profiles.source_text: Standardized islet autoantibody tests are recommended for classification of diabetes in adults who have phenotypic risk factors that overlap with those for type 1 diabetes (e.g., younger age at diagnosis, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, or short time to insulin treatment). E
comorbidities: phenotypic risk factors for type 1 diabetes

patient_profiles.name: Individuals treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)
patient_profiles.source_text: People starting cancer treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including anti-PD-1 or anti-PDL-1 therapy (e.g., nivolumab, pembrolizumab, avelumab), phosphoinositidyl 3-kinase α (PI3Kα) inhibitors (e.g., alpelisib, inavolisib), or mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors (e.g., everolimus), should be educated regarding risks, symptoms, and signs of hyperglycemia and hyperglycemic crises.

patient_profiles.name: Individuals treated with PI3Kα inhibitors
patient_profiles.source_text: In people treated with PI3Kα inhibitors, fasting or random plasma glucose and A1C should be tested before initiating treatment, and random plasma glucose should be tested weekly for the first 2 weeks of treatment and then every 4 weeks during treatment. Consider testing A1C every 3 months during treatment.

patient_profiles.name: Individuals treated with mTOR inhibitors
patient_profiles.source_text: In people treated with mTOR inhibitors, fasting or random plasma glucose should be tested before starting and at each visit throughout the duration of treatment. Consider testing A1C every 3 months during treatment.

patient_profiles.name: People with pancreatitis
patient_profiles.source_text: For people with pancreatitis and diabetes, glucose-lowering therapies potentially associated with increased risk of pancreatitis (i.e., incretin-based therapies) should be avoided.

patient_profiles.name: People with chronic pancreatitis
patient_profiles.source_text: Screen people for diabetes within 3–6 months following an episode of acute pancreatitis and annually thereafter. Screening for diabetes is recommended annually for people with chronic pancreatitis. E

patient_profiles.name: People with cystic fibrosis
patient_profiles.source_text: Annual screening for cystic fibrosis–related diabetes (CFRD) should begin by age 10 years in all people with cystic fibrosis, preferably using OGTT. B

patient_profiles.name: Organ transplant recipients
patient_profiles.source_text: After organ transplantation, screening for hyperglycemia should be done. A formal diagnosis of post-transplantation diabetes mellitus (PTDM) is best made once the individual is stable on an immunosuppressive plan (usually 3 months) and in the absence of acute infection (158,161–163,166).

patient_profiles.name: Individuals diagnosed with diabetes in the first 6 months of life
patient_profiles.source_text: Regardless of current age, all people diagnosed with diabetes in the first 6 months of life should have genetic testing for neonatal diabetes.

patient_profiles.name: Children and young adults with a family history of diabetes in successive generations
